title: Acute appendicitis (adult)
subject: surgery-trauma
setting: Emergency department, surgical ward, operating theatre
summary: Stratify risk with the AIR or Alvarado score, image intermediate-risk patients (ultrasound first, low-dose CT if negative), and perform laparoscopic appendicectomy within 24 hours with a single preoperative antibiotic dose; antibiotic-first treatment is an option for selected uncomplicated cases without an appendicolith (WSES 2020).

sections.title: Recognise
items: Classic picture: central abdominal pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, nausea or vomiting, low-grade fever, and RIF tenderness with guarding or rebound.
Presentation is often atypical in older adults, pregnancy (pain may be higher), and with a retrocaecal or pelvic appendix; perforation risk rises with delay.
Differentials: ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion or cyst, pelvic inflammatory disease, ureteric colic, mesenteric adenitis, Crohn disease, and in India ileocaecal tuberculosis and typhoid enteritis.
Always do a pregnancy test in women of reproductive age.

sections.title: Scores and imaging
items: Alvarado score (0 to 10): migration of pain 1, anorexia 1, nausea or vomiting 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 1, temperature 37.3°C or more 1, leucocytosis 2, neutrophilia 1. Useful to exclude appendicitis; do not use it to confirm the diagnosis in adults.
AIR score (0 to 12): low risk 0 to 4, intermediate 5 to 8, high 9 to 12. WSES recommends the AIR or Adult Appendicitis Score for risk stratification.
Low risk: observation or discharge with safety-netting. Intermediate risk: timely imaging. High risk and under 40 years: CT may be omitted before diagnostic or therapeutic laparoscopy.
Ultrasound (point-of-care or formal) first; if negative or inconclusive, contrast-enhanced low-dose CT. In pregnancy: graded compression ultrasound, then MRI if inconclusive.
Bloods: FBC, CRP, electrolytes, creatinine; urinalysis; beta-hCG.
CT features of complicated disease (appendicolith, abscess, extraluminal air, phlegmon) change management; an appendicolith predicts failure of antibiotic-only treatment.

sections.title: Operative management
items: Laparoscopic appendicectomy is preferred for both uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis, including in obese, older and pregnant patients, where expertise and equipment are available.
Operate on the next available list within 24 hours of admission for uncomplicated appendicitis; avoid delay beyond 24 hours.

Give a single preoperative dose of broad-spectrum antibiotic within 60 minutes before incision, for example cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV. No postoperative antibiotics for uncomplicated appendicitis.
Complicated appendicitis (gangrene, perforation, abscess): postoperative antibiotics for no longer than 3 to 5 days when source control is adequate; suction alone for collections, no routine drains.
Remove an appendix that looks normal if no other cause is found, and send every specimen for histopathology.

sections.title: Non-operative (antibiotic-first) management
items: Discuss as a safe alternative for selected adults with imaging-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis and no appendicolith; explain the risk of failure, missed complicated disease, and recurrence of up to 39% at 5 years.
Not recommended in pregnancy.
Start IV antibiotics and switch to oral when improving; most trials gave at least 48 hours IV then oral, for a total of 7 to 10 days.

Empirical IV options (WSES, community-acquired intra-abdominal infection): ceftriaxone 2 g once daily plus metronidazole 500 mg every 6 to 8 hours, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g every 6 to 8 hours; ertapenem 1 g once daily if ESBL risk. Choose oral step-down by the local antibiogram.
Worsening pain, peritonitis, sepsis or no improvement on IV antibiotics means proceed to appendicectomy.

sections.title: Appendicular mass or abscess
items: Abscess: antibiotics with percutaneous drainage where available if laparoscopic expertise is lacking; laparoscopic surgery is the treatment of choice where advanced expertise exists, with a low threshold for conversion.
No routine interval appendicectomy after successful non-operative treatment in patients under 40; offer it for recurrent symptoms.
Age 40 or over treated non-operatively: colonoscopy and interval contrast-enhanced CT to exclude neoplasm.

sections.title: Pregnancy, older adults and children
items: Pregnancy: lab tests are always needed alongside examination; ultrasound then MRI; laparoscopic appendicectomy when indicated, with obstetric input.
Older adults: higher perforation rate and higher chance of an underlying neoplasm; low threshold for CT and follow-up colonoscopy.
Children: do not diagnose on scores alone; use ultrasound first and avoid routine CT as first-line imaging (WSES 2020).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using the Alvarado score to confirm rather than exclude appendicitis.
Missing ectopic pregnancy or ovarian torsion in young women.
Continuing antibiotics after uncomplicated appendicectomy, or beyond 5 days after adequate source control.
Offering antibiotic-only treatment when an appendicolith is present.
Delaying surgery beyond 24 hours in patients who need it.

drugs.name: Cefazolin plus metronidazole (prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more) plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, single dose within 60 minutes before incision
drugs.notes: Redose cefazolin if surgery exceeds 4 hours.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: Combine with metronidazole for non-operative or complicated appendicitis.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.notes: Check local E. coli resistance before using as monotherapy.

drugs.name: Ertapenem
drugs.notes: Reserve for ESBL risk; reduce dose if creatinine clearance is 30 mL/min or less.
